For sufficiently large fixed $a$, $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-a}$, and finite scaled source half-Hölder norm, the formal statement gives finiteness of the velocity norm and $\|v\|_{[n],1/2}\le C_n\mathsf D^C\|g\|_{[n],1/2}$ for all $n\ge0$. The norms sum scaled label derivatives on the whole interval, with the maximum of the supremum and half-Hölder seminorm at each order. The exponent $C$ is chosen after $a$ but before the parent and derivative order.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Text.eq_5_59: For every integer $m\ge0$, there is a constant $C_m$ independent of the real normed spaces $E,F,G$ and the continuous bilinear map $B:E\times F\to G$, such that $f,g\in C^{m,1/2}(\mathbb R^3)$ imply $B(f,g)\in C^{m,1/2}$ and $\|B(f,g)\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le C_m\|B\|\|f\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\|g\|_{C^{m,1/2}}$. This theorem proves the formal assertion corresponding to (5.59), with all target-space and product choices included. The proof permits $C_m=3(m+1)2^m$. Scalar multiplication and the tensor products used in the cutoff residual are special cases; no periodicity assumption is needed.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Text.eq_D_2: Let $0<\ell_*\le1$ and let $c:I\times\mathbb R^3\to X$ be smooth in the label variable, where $X$ is any real normed space. Assume all derivatives through order $n+1$ are uniformly bounded in time and label. The formal statement proves $\|c\|_{[n]}\le\|c\|_{[n],1/2}\le4\ell_*^{-1/2}\|c\|_{[n+1]}$ and establishes finiteness of the Hölder quantities. At an order $m$ with derivatives bounded through $m+1$, it also proves $\ell_*^m|c|_{m,1/2}\le4\ell_*^{-1/2}(\ell_*^m|c|_m+\ell_*^{m+1}|c|_{m+1})$. Each multi-index is counted once. The Hölder norm uses the maximum of supremum and seminorm; their sum is equivalent within a factor two. Thus the explicit constant four yields the paper's unspecified constant after the chosen norm convention is accounted for.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Text.section8_setting: This theorem proves that there are admissible parameters, an inductive construction, a constant and a finite positive time $T_\infty$ satisfying Theorem 7.1. The same smooth periodic stage velocities have the stated residual, support, increment and central-wave bounds, and their activation times converge to $T_\infty$ while each stage lasts beyond it. This supplies the setting selected at the start of Section 8. The formal conclusion stops at that existence assertion: it does not introduce $w$ or assert uniform convergence on the closed interval. The continuous terminal velocity is established by a separate result using summability of the increments.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Theorem71Conclusions: For smooth odd periodic velocities $U_j$ on $[0,S_j]\times\mathbb R^3$, their flows $X_j$, zero-mean pressures $\pi_j$ and residuals $R_j$, this condition requires frequency support $\le2\lambda_j^5$, $\|U_j\|_\infty,\|(D_aX_j)^{\pm1}\|_\infty\le\lambda_j$, $\|R_j\|_\infty\le\lambda_{j+1}^{-3}$ and $D^2\pi_j\le(\sum_{i<j}\lambda_i^{-1})I$. At the origin, the central splitting has error $\le\lambda_j^{-1/4}$; at $t_{j+1}$, $\eta_j/\nu_j=\varepsilon_j$, $\pi\le\nu_j\le4\pi$ and $C^{-1}\lambda_j^{1/4}\le\sigma_j\le C\lambda_j^{1/4}L_{j+1}^2$, with $C\ge2$. Times satisfy $0=t_1=t_2<t_3<\cdots\to T_\infty\in(0,S_j)$. At each time, oscillations are supported within distance $\lambda_{j-1}^{-1}$ of the integer lattice, with $\|O_j\|_\infty\le\lambda_j^{-1}$ and $\|U_j-U_{j-1}-O_j\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le\lambda_j^{-1}$ for $m\le q_j$; $O_j=0$ before activation for $j\ge2$. These requirements neither construct the fields nor identify the oscillation with the finite expansion. Continuity in the time-dependent Hölder norm is not separately asserted. The spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ norm is $\sum_{i\le m}(\sup|D^if|+[D^if]_{1/2})$, where $D^if$ is the full $i$th derivative tensor in operator norm.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Theorem71StepData: For wave $j\ge1$, take parent $U_{j-1}$ on $[0,S_j]$, frequency $\lambda_j$, parent bound $\mathsf D=\lambda_{j-1}^9$, envelope radius $\mathsf D^{-a}$ and depth $P=6K_{j+1}$. The formal condition requires the parent and central estimates of §5.1, a transported phase, the projected seed at every label, and the finite expansion satisfying its equations. It identifies $V=U_{j-1}+W^\natural$, its approximate Euler equation, $U_j=S_{\lambda_j^5}V$, and $O_j=(W-\langle W\rangle)^\natural$ on $[0,S_j]$. Fields are periodic lifts to $\mathbb R^3$; physical evaluation uses the inverse parent flow. The seed at the origin is identified with $\mathbf a_j$ on $[t_j,S_j]$. No corresponding identification of $\kappa_j$ with $(D_aX_{j-1})^{-T}k_*$ is recorded. This declaration specifies requirements for given step data; it does not prove their existence.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Theorem71Steps: Fix a construction, a nonnegative integer envelope exponent $a$ and a Fourier cutoff symbol $\psi$. The formal condition asserts that, for every wave index $j\ge1$, there exist the phase, seed, time cutoff and finite expansion that realize step $j$ over $U_{j-1}$ on $[0,S_j]$. The expansion uses $\mathsf D=\lambda_{j-1}^9$, radius $\mathsf D^{-a}$ and depth $6K_{j+1}$; its physical evaluation produces $V$, $U_j=S_{\lambda_j^5}V$ and $O_j=W_{\rm osc}^\natural$. Thus one $a$ and one symbol serve all steps, while the profiles may vary with $j$. The central seed agrees with $\mathbf a_j$, but equality of the transported covector with $\kappa_j$ is not a required clause. The numbered theorem proves this condition for its constructed sequence.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.WaveOn: For paths $k,\mathbf a$ and a prescribed linear map $D(t)$ on a time set $J$, the formal condition is $k'=-D^Tk$ and $\mathbf a'=-D\mathbf a+2(k\cdot D\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$ at every time in $J$. Derivatives are taken relative to $J$, allowing one-sided endpoint derivatives. This includes the first three relations of (2.1), but not its final condition $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$. Nonvanishing, zero trace, pressure compatibility and regularity of $D$ are also separate assumptions. Division by zero is assigned zero, so the equations are defined even for $k=0$; the nonzero physical-wave interpretation requires additional data.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.alpha: For the preceding wave’s orthonormal frame, set $\sigma=|k_p(t_0)||\mathbf a_p(t_0)|$, $\nu=B_{12}(t_0)>0$, $r=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}$ and $S=\sigma/r$. At physical time $t=t_0+\tau/r$, the formal vector is $\alpha=(S E_1\cdot\mathbf a,E_2\cdot\mathbf a,S E_3\cdot\mathbf a)$. Thus $\mathbf a=\alpha_1E_1/S+\alpha_2E_2+\alpha_3E_3/S$, as in (2.3). Forming these coordinates does not impose the amplitude equation or transversality. The formula accepts every real $\tau$; the frame hypotheses and differential equations are guaranteed only where the physical time lies in the supplied compact set. Earlier intermediate formulas use the negative first component instead.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.corollary_8_3: Assume the common construction of Theorem 7.1, its smooth odd Euler limit from Proposition 8.1, and the formal Proposition 8.2 conclusions, including a uniform lower bound $c\lambda_{j-1}^{1/8}-C\lambda_{j-1}^{1/32}-C$ for central vorticity on every late activation interval. The theorem proves that $T_\infty>0$ is the maximal lifespan, that every maximal solution of finite lifespan from the same data has that time, and that both integrals in (1.2) diverge. The norms are essential suprema over a unit cell, with the operator norm for $\nabla u$. The conclusion agrees with Corollary 8.3. Its formal proof uses the quantitative vorticity and crossing-time estimates; it does not prove the periodic Beale–Kato–Majda continuation criterion cited by the paper.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_1_3: Let $b\ge1$ be an integer, $K(s)=320b(s+1)$, and $\mathcal B(s)>0$ satisfy $\log\mathcal B(s)\ge4K(s+1)^3$ for $s\ge1$. Suppose $\lambda_0\ge\mathcal B(1)$, $q_1=1$, $\lambda_j=\lambda_{j-1}^{K(q_j)}$, and $q_{j+1}=\max\{1\le s\le q_j+1:\mathcal B(s)\le\lambda_{j-1}\}$. Then $q_j\le q_{j+1}\le q_j+1$, $q_j\to\infty$, and $4\log\lambda_{j+2}\le(\log\lambda_{j-1})^2$ for $j\ge1$. Thus the last expression is exactly (1.15), since $L_{j+1}=4\log\lambda_{j+2}$. The formal statement omits threshold monotonicity and analytic-cost domination from §1.5; the arithmetic result therefore applies under fewer assumptions.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_1: Let $J$ be a time interval on which relative derivatives are uniquely determined. Suppose $D$ is differentiable, $\operatorname{tr}D=0$, $D'+D^2$ is symmetric, and $k'=-D^Tk$, $\mathbf a'=-D\mathbf a+p_{\rm w}k$, where $p_{\rm w}=2k\cdot D\mathbf a/|k|^2$. For differentiable $F$ and any $P$ with $P'=F$, transverse data give an Euler velocity $u=Dx+\mathbf aF(k\cdot x)$ on $\mathbb R^3$, with pressure $-x\cdot(D'+D^2)x/2-p_{\rm w}P(k\cdot x)$ and zero divergence. Nonzero perpendicular data at any $t_0\in J$ remain so throughout $J$, including earlier times. Unlike the paper, the formal statement requires neither a smooth odd periodic profile nor its normalization; the Euler identity also allows $k=0$, using zero for division by zero. The interval derivative includes one-sided endpoint derivatives.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_2: Let nonzero perpendicular paths $k,\mathbf a\in\mathbb R^3$ satisfy $k'=-B^Tk$ and $\mathbf a'=-B\mathbf a+2(k\cdot B\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$ on a time set $J$, with $\operatorname{tr}B=0$. Put $E_1=k/|k|$, $E_2=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$, $E_3=E_1\times E_2$, $B_{ij}=E_i\cdot BE_j$ and $\sigma=|k||\mathbf a|$. The formal statement gives orthonormality and $E_1'=-B_{12}E_2-B_{13}E_3$, $E_2'=B_{12}E_1-B_{32}E_3$, $E_3'=B_{13}E_1+B_{32}E_2$, $(\log\sigma)'=B_{33}$. Derivatives are relative to $J$. These are (2.2), with no regularity assumption on $B$ beyond the supplied wave derivatives and no symmetry assumption on $B'+B^2$. All normalizations and the logarithm have nonzero positive denominators or arguments under the stated hypotheses.

notes.TorusEuler.Paper.meanDeformation: For the two-time flow notation $X(s,t,a)$, this definition is $F(t,a)=D_aX(0,t,a)$, a linear map on Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$. notes.TorusEuler.Paper.meanDeformationInv: The formal definition is $G(t,a)=D_xX(t,0,x)|_{x=X(0,t,a)}$. This is the inverse deformation in §3.1 and the coefficient of the derivative $\mathbf d=G^T\nabla_a$. The displayed definition accepts arbitrary maps and does not itself prove the inverse identity. notes.TorusEuler.Paper.meanGradient: For a velocity $U$ and two-time maps $X$, the formal definition is $M(t,a)=D_xU(t,X(0,t,a))$. The definition alone imposes no Euler equation, incompressibility or trajectory equation. At a spatial nondifferentiability point the formal derivative is assigned zero; the paper's smoothness assumptions ensure the usual gradient is used.

This expression defines its time derivative with the label $a$ fixed, taken within $[0,T]$. At $t=0$ and $t=T$ it is the corresponding one-sided derivative. This is the $M_t$ in (4.1), not the derivative at fixed Eulerian position. If the derivative within the interval does not exist, the formal expression is assigned zero. This convention is irrelevant under the smooth-parent assumptions of §4 with $T>0$, which ensure the ordinary one-sided derivative at the endpoints and the usual derivative in the interior.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.meanHsharp: For $M(t,a)=D_xu(t,X_{0,t}(a))$, define $H^\#(t,a)=-(M_t(t,a)+M(t,a)^2)$, with time differentiation at fixed label within $[0,T]$. This is precisely the coefficient in (4.1). No symmetry is built into the definition. If $u$ solves Euler, (4.3) identifies it with the pressure Hessian along the flow; for a parent with residual $R$, the additional term is $-(\nabla R)\circ X$. The inverse requires the upper quadratic-form bound $H^\#\le I$, which is a separate assumption.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.meanKinetic: For a differentiable particle map $a\mapsto X_{0,t}(a)$, write $F=D_aX_{0,t}(a)$. The coefficient is $K=F^TF$, so $Kw\cdot w=|Fw|^2$. It is the kinetic matrix in (4.1), and the quadratic part of the label energy in (4.7). The transpose is the Euclidean adjoint and norms are operator norms. This definition gives nonnegativity, not a positive lower bound. If $F$ has inverse norm at most $D_->0$, the separate ellipticity estimate gives $K\ge D_-^{-2}I$.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.meanVorticity: With $F=D_aX_{0,t}(a)$ and $M=D_xu(t,X_{0,t}(a))$, the coefficient is $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$. It is the pulled-back vorticity in (4.1) and supplies the term $\Omega z_t\cdot z$ in the endpoint energy. The matrix convention is $(D_xu)_{ij}=\partial_ju_i$, fixing the sign of $M^T-M$. The formula does not require Euler or incompressibility. Its relation $K_t-\Omega=2F^TF_t$ uses the separately established flow identity $F_t=MF$.

notes.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_5_4: Assume a smooth odd unit-periodic solenoidal parent and smooth periodic pressure on $0<T\le1$, with bands $2\mathsf D$ for velocity and $4\mathsf D$ for its odd residual, gradient and both deformation bounds $\mathsf D\ge2$, residual bound $\lambda^{-5/2}$ and $D^2p_U-DR_U\le I$. Put $M=DU\circ X$, $\kappa=DX^{-T}k_*$, $\lambda=|\kappa(t_0,0)|\ge1$ and $0\le t_0<T$. The nonzero central seed solves $\mathbf a_t=-(I-2P_\kappa)M\mathbf a$, is transverse, has $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a\ge\mathsf D^{-1}|\kappa||\mathbf a|$, and satisfies $0<\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|\le1$. Every transverse homogeneous solution $\mathbf b$ obeys $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$ for $t_0\le t'\le t\le T$. The oscillations and their sources vanish before activation and, at all times, outside the envelope; outside the envelope the remainder $R_P$ is also phase independent. notes.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_8_1: For every common construction satisfying Theorem 7.1, this theorem constructs smooth periodic velocity $u$ and mean-zero pressure $p$ solving Euler on $[0,T_\infty)$. The datum $u(0)$ is smooth, odd and divergence free, with $U_j(0)\to u(0)$ in every $C^{m,1/2}$. The velocity stays odd, and $U_j\to u$ uniformly in each such spatial norm on every $[0,S]$, $S<T_\infty$. Every maximal solution of finite lifespan from the same data lasts at least to $T_\infty$ and agrees with $u$ there. This is a conditional comparison, not general maximal-solution existence; Corollary 8.3 later proves maximality of the constructed solution. The spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ norm is $\sum_{i\le m}(\sup|D^if|+[D^if]_{1/2})$, where $D^if$ is the full $i$th derivative tensor in operator norm.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_8_2: For a common construction satisfying Theorem 7.1 and its smooth Euler limit from Proposition 8.1, this theorem proves $\sup_{0\le t<T_\infty}\|u(t)\|_\infty<\infty$ and $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$. In addition, fixed real $c>0,C$ give $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\ge c\lambda_{j-1}^{1/8}-C\lambda_{j-1}^{1/32}-C$ for every sufficiently large $j$ and all $t\in[t_j,t_{j+1})$. Thus the blow-up is not restricted to a sequence of times. The spatial domain is the unit torus, represented by periodic fields on $\mathbb R^3$; the velocity norm is its essential supremum. The quantitative estimate is stronger than the printed Proposition 8.2 and is used with crossing lengths for the later integral argument.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_8_4: For the smooth periodic Euler limit of any common construction satisfying Theorem 7.1, this theorem proves the two limits in Proposition 8.4. Given a compact $K\subset\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb Z^3$ and an integer $m\ge0$, $u(t)$ and $\partial_tu(t)$ converge uniformly on $K$ with every spatial derivative through order $m$, as $t\uparrow T_\infty$. The limits extend to $C^m$ fields near $K$. Removing the lattice means removing the torus origin, and the time derivative is taken inside $[0,T_\infty)$. The conclusion supplies spatial limits of the velocity and one time derivative; it does not require convergence of all higher time derivatives. The auxiliary note proves a stronger extension assertion for a suitably chosen construction.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.referenceAmplitude: For a real function $Y$ and time $\tau$, the formal expression is $a_{\rm ref}(\tau)=\exp(\int_0^\tau Y(s)\,ds)$, using the interval integral with its orientation when $\tau<0$. This defines a positive number for every input function. If the integral is not defined by an integrable function on the interval, the formal integral is assigned zero, giving amplitude one; this is not a claim of integrability. In the application, $Y$ solves (2.12) on $[0,\infty)$, hence is continuous there, and the ordinary integral gives the reference amplitude with $a_{\rm ref}(0)=1$ and $a_{\rm ref}'=Ya_{\rm ref}$.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.referenceAngle: The formal angle is $\varphi(\tau)=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$ for every real $\varepsilon,\tau$. It satisfies $\tan\varphi=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$, and for $\varepsilon\ge0$ lies in $[0,\pi/2)$. These specify the branch in (2.4); there is no ambiguity by integer multiples of $\pi$. The angle parametrizes the limiting direction $\tan\varphi E_1+E_3$ as the preceding shear tends to infinity. The definition does not claim that it is the actual angle of a finite-shear or perturbed wave, whose components must be estimated separately.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.referenceAngle_mem: For every $\varepsilon\ge0$ and every real $\tau$, the formal statement proves $0\le\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)<\pi/2$. This is the branch requirement for $\varphi$ in (2.4), extended to all real times. In particular the cosine is positive at every finite time. The result concerns the explicitly defined reference angle only; it does not constrain the actual wave vector of a finite-shear configuration. Neither an evolution equation nor the smallness condition (2.7) is a hypothesis.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.referenceSystemMatrix: Put $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$. The formal matrix acting on $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ is $-\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\varepsilon\tau\sin2\varphi&\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$. Its second row therefore gives $\alpha_2'=-\alpha_1$, exactly as in (2.5). This definition uses the paper’s signs, unlike the intermediate matrix in coordinates $(-\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$. It is defined for all real parameters and times and is only a coefficient matrix: it neither constructs a solution nor proves that a particular amplitude satisfies the equation. Those assertions require separate differential-equation hypotheses or theorems.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.remark_1_2: There exist smooth odd divergence-free data $u_0$ on $\mathbb T^3$ and a smooth odd maximal Euler solution on $[0,T_*)$, with $0<T_*<\infty$, bounded velocity, $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$, and divergent time integrals of both gradient and vorticity norms. Velocity and its time derivative converge in every spatial $C^m$ norm on compact sets away from the origin. The velocity also extends smoothly in space and time through $T_*$ away from that point. Any maximal solution of finite real lifespan from $u_0$ has the same lifespan and velocity. The extension is periodic and need not solve Euler after $T_*$. This is the existential assertion of Remark 1.2, not an extension theorem for every singular solution.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.scaledNormSq: For a real scale $S$ and vector $\zeta\in\mathbb R^3$, the formal expression is $m=\zeta_1^2+\zeta_2^2/S^2+\zeta_3^2$. When $S\ne0$ and $k=\lambda(\zeta_1E_1+\zeta_2E_2/S+\zeta_3E_3)$ in an orthonormal frame, it satisfies $|k|^2=\lambda^2m$. This is the factor after (2.3), not the ordinary Euclidean squared norm of $\zeta$. The definition also permits $S=0$: division by zero is assigned zero, so the middle term vanishes. To use $m$ as a nonzero pressure denominator, the amplitude equations impose positive $S$ and nonzero $\zeta_3$.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.strongShearMatrix: For scale $S$, ratio $\varepsilon$ and scaled wave vector $\zeta$, put $m=\zeta_1^2+\zeta_2^2/S^2+\zeta_3^2$ and $\Pi=(2\zeta_2\alpha_1+(\zeta_1+\varepsilon\zeta_3)\alpha_2)/m$. The formal matrix is the linear map whose first component is $-\alpha_2+\zeta_1\Pi$ and whose second is $-(1-1/(2S^2))\alpha_1+\varepsilon(\zeta_1\alpha_1+\zeta_2\alpha_2)/(2S^2\zeta_3)+\zeta_2\Pi/S^2$. These are the finite-shear right-hand sides in Lemma 2.3. The definition asserts no differential equation. Its use for a model amplitude requires $S>0$, $\zeta_3\ne0$ and transversality. At zero denominators the formal divisions are assigned zero, so existence of the matrix alone does not establish that this reduction is valid.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.strongShearMatrix_mulVe: Let $m=\zeta_1^2+\zeta_2^2/S^2+\zeta_3^2$ and $\Pi=(2\zeta_2\alpha_1+(\zeta_1+\varepsilon\zeta_3)\alpha_2)/m$. The formal statement proves that the finite-shear matrix applied to $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ has components $-\alpha_2+\zeta_1\Pi$ and $-(1-1/(2S^2))\alpha_1+\varepsilon(\zeta_1\alpha_1+\zeta_2\alpha_2)/(2S^2\zeta_3)+\zeta_2\Pi/S^2$. This verifies the algebra connecting the coefficient matrix to Lemma 2.3. The identity holds for arbitrary real inputs, including zero denominators because every division by zero is assigned zero. It is not an assertion that an amplitude solves this system; that requires the model wave hypotheses and $\zeta_3\ne0$.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.strongShearPressure: For $S,\varepsilon\in\mathbb R$ and $\zeta\in\mathbb R^3$, the formal formula is $\Pi=(2\zeta_2\alpha_1+(\zeta_1+\varepsilon\zeta_3)\alpha_2)/(\zeta_1^2+\zeta_2^2/S^2+\zeta_3^2)$. In the two-entry model, with positive $S$, nonzero wave vector and the scaling (2.3), this is $\lambda S p_{\rm w}/r$. It is the pressure term in Lemma 2.3, linear in the two remaining amplitude components. The definition itself does not assume the model equations or positivity of the denominator. Division by zero is assigned zero; the lemma’s condition $\zeta_3\ne0$ ensures the ordinary pressure interpretation.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.tan_referenceAngle: For all real $\varepsilon,\tau$, the formal statement proves $\tan(\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2))=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$. This is the first relation in (2.4) with the explicitly chosen arctangent branch. It imposes no sign condition on $\varepsilon$ and involves no wave equation. The additional paper condition $0\le\varphi<\pi/2$ uses $\varepsilon\ge0$. Because arctangent always lies strictly between $-\pi/2$ and $\pi/2$, the tangent here does not encounter a pole at any finite real input.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_1_1: There exist smooth odd divergence-free periodic data $u_0$ and a smooth odd maximal Euler solution $u,p$ on $[0,T_*)$, with finite $T_*>0$. Velocity remains uniformly bounded, $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$, and the time integrals of $\|\nabla u(t)\|_\infty$ and $\|\operatorname{curl}u(t)\|_\infty$ both diverge. For every compact set away from the torus origin and every $m\ge0$, velocity and its time derivative converge in $C^m$. The formal statement further spells out the classical uniqueness implicit in the paper: every maximal solution from $u_0$ has endpoint $T_*$ and agrees with $u$ before it. Fields are periodic functions on $\mathbb R^3$; pressure has zero spatial mean.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_4_2: On $I=[0,T]$, $0<T\le1$, let $U$ be smooth, unit-periodic and divergence free, $X$ its flow from time zero, $F=D_aX$, $M=(DU)\circ X$, $K=F^TF$, $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$, and $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)\le I$ as quadratic forms. Assume $\|F^{-1}\|_\infty\le D\ge1$, $\|M\|_\infty\le L$, $\|K\|_\infty\le K_0$, $\|D_aK\|_\infty\le K_1$, $\|\Omega\|_\infty\le\Omega_0$, $\|D_a\Omega\|_\infty\le\Omega_1$, with nonnegative bounds. For $L_{\rm src}\in C(I;C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb T^3))$, solve $Kv-J(\Omega v)+L_{\rm src}=c+G_\phi$, $z_t=v$, $z(0)=z(T)=0$, where $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$. The fields $z,v,c$ are weakly divergence free; $z\in C^1_tC^{0,1/2}$, $v,G_\phi\in C_tC^{0,1/2}$, and $G_\phi=\nabla_a\phi$ for a periodic potential at each time. There are absolute $C\ge0$ and an integer $p\ge0$ such that $A=C(D+L+K_0+K_1+\Omega_0+\Omega_1)^p$ gives $\|v\|_{C_tC^{0,1/2}}\le A\|L_{\rm src}\|_{C_tC^{0,1/2}}$ and $\|(\mathbb PK(t))^{-1}\mathbb P\|\le A$ uniformly on $I$. The solution is unique in $z,v,c,G_\phi$ on $I$, not in the potential. Smooth force sources $L_{\rm src}=-J(F^T(f\circ X))$ also give smooth solutions of the linearized Euler equation. The coefficient bound uses first derivative suprema rather than full $C^{1,1/2}$ norms.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_5_6: On $0<T\le1$, assume smooth odd periodic solenoidal $U$ with flow $X$, smooth periodic $p_U$, Fourier bands $2\mathsf D,4\mathsf D$ for $U,R_U=U_t+DU\,U+\nabla p_U$, odd $R_U$, $\|DU\|,\|DX\|,\|DX^{-1}\|\le\mathsf D\ge2$, $\|R_U\|\le\lambda^{-5/2}$ and $D^2p_U-DR_U\le I$. Put $M=DU\circ X$, $\kappa=DX^{-T}k_*$, $|\kappa(t_0,0)|=\lambda\ge1$, $0\le t_0<T$. Require a nonzero transverse homogeneous seed, $0<\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|\le1$, $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a\ge\mathsf D^{-1}|\kappa||\mathbf a|$, and $|b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|b(t')|/\gamma(t')$ for every transverse homogeneous $b$ and $t_0\le t'\le t\le T$. At fixed sufficiently small $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-a}$, if $\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$, a depth-$P\ge2$ expansion obeys: $V_1,\lambda\mathsf p_1=O(\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-5/4})$; $V_p,f_p+f_p^S,\lambda\mathsf p_p=O(\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-5/4-2(p-1)/3})$ and $B_p,\bar f_p=O(\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-5/2-2(p-2)/3})$ for $2\le p\le P$; $C_{p+1}=O(\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-9/4-2(p-1)/3})$ for $1\le p\le P$. These hold in every finite scaled derivative norm, weighted by $\gamma^{-1}$ on the active interval for oscillations and unweighted on $[0,T]$ for means. Constants may depend on order and level or depth, but are uniform in the parent; one exponent works throughout. Homogeneous means $b_t=-(I-2P_\kappa)Mb$, with $P_\kappa=\kappa\otimes\kappa/|\kappa|^2$. Also $W_{\rm osc}=O(\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-5/4})$, $\sum_{p=2}^PB_p,\sum_{p=2}^P\bar f_p=O(\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-5/2})$, and $\|R_P\|_{[m]}\le C_{m,P}\lambda^{-5/4-2P/3}$.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_7_1: For each smooth radial Fourier cutoff and integer $a_0$, the theorem chooses $b\ge1$, an envelope exponent $a\ge a_0$ and fixed-order majorants. Every admissible threshold $\mathcal B$ above them permits construction for all sufficiently large $N$. It gives smooth odd divergence-free periodic velocities on $[0,S_j]\times\mathbb R^3$, starting from $\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+\varepsilon_1e_3)$, with $\|U_j\|_\infty,\|(D_aX_j)^{\pm1}\|_\infty\le\lambda_j$, $\|R_j\|_\infty\le\lambda_{j+1}^{-3}$ and $D^2\pi_j\le(\sum_{i<j}\lambda_i^{-1})I$. The central splitting has error $\le\lambda_j^{-1/4}$; at $t_{j+1}$, $\eta_j/\nu_j=\varepsilon_j$, $\pi\le\nu_j\le4\pi$ and $C^{-1}\lambda_j^{1/4}\le\sigma_j\le C\lambda_j^{1/4}L_{j+1}^2$, with $C=18e^3$. Also $t_j\to T_\infty\in(0,S_j)$ and $\|O_j\|_\infty,\|U_j-U_{j-1}-O_j\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le\lambda_j^{-1}$ for $m\le q_j$. Each step equals its finite expansion and Fourier cutoff. The central seed is identified, but equality of central and transported covectors and first-wave initial directions and normalization are absent. Hölder bounds are pointwise in time, in the spatial norm $\sum_{i\le m}(\sup|D^if|+[D^if]_{1/2})$, with $D^if$ the full $i$th derivative tensor. The exponent can be chosen arbitrarily large; the assertion does not cover every sufficiently large exponent.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_A_1: There are constants $C\ge0$ and $p\in\mathbb N$, chosen before the data. On $[0,1]\times\mathbb T^3$, let symmetric $K$ and skew-symmetric $\Omega$ be time-continuous in $C^{0,1/2}$ and spatially differentiable, with uniform value and first derivative bounds $K_0,K_1,\Omega_0,\Omega_1$. Assume $K\ge\kappa I$, $\kappa>0$, and $\int_0^1(Kz_t\cdot z_t+\Omega z_t\cdot z)\,dt\ge\mu\int_0^1|z_t|^2\,dt$ for every $H^1_0$ path at every label, with $\mu>0$. Each $L\in C_tC^{0,1/2}$ gives unique $z,v=z_t,c,G$ on this interval satisfying $Kv-J(\Omega v)+L=c+G$, $z(0)=z(1)=0$, with solenoidal $z,c$ and periodic $G=\nabla\phi$. Moreover $\|v\|_0\le CQ^p\|L\|_0$, where $Q=2+\kappa^{-1}+\mu^{-1}+K_0+K_1+\Omega_0+\Omega_1$ and $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw$. Smooth data give smooth $z,c,G$. The norm is the time supremum of the spatial half-Hölder norm. The paper assumes stronger coefficient regularity; the scalar potential is not unique.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.zeta: At physical time $t=t_0+\tau/r$, the formal vector is $\zeta=((E_1\cdot k)/\lambda,S(E_2\cdot k)/\lambda,(E_3\cdot k)/\lambda)$, where $r=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}$ and $S=\sigma/r$ use the positive activation strength and coupling of the preceding wave. In an orthonormal frame and for $\lambda\ne0$, this is exactly the wave-vector expansion (2.3). No new wave equation or initial frequency condition is imposed by this definition. It accepts $\lambda=0$, in which case all three divisions are assigned zero. The amplification theorems separately require $\lambda>0$ and physical times inside the compact set on which the frame assumptions hold.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.zetaRef: For real $\varepsilon,\tau$, the formal vector is $\zeta_0=(\tan\varphi,-\varepsilon\tau,1)=(\varepsilon\tau^2/2,-\varepsilon\tau,1)$, with $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$. This defines the reference coordinates in (2.4), and its initial value is $(0,0,1)$. The third component is identically one. The definition does not by itself state its differential equations or convergence of an actual wave to it. Those are separate calculations. Its norm is the Euclidean norm of these three coordinates; it is not the physical wave vector, whose second component also carries $S^{-1}$ in (2.3).
notes.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.WaveOn: For functions $k,\mathbf a$ and a prescribed spatial linear map $D(t)$ on a time set $J$, the formal condition requires $k'=-D^Tk$ and $\mathbf a'=-D\mathbf a+2(k\cdot D\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$ throughout $J$. The second equation is expressed as a linear operator applied to $\mathbf a$. Derivatives are relative to $J$, including one-sided derivatives when $J$ is an interval with endpoints. Transversality, nonzero vectors and the background Euler conditions are absent from this condition and must be imposed separately. Division by zero is assigned zero, so the displayed right-hand side is formally defined even when $k=0$.

notes.TorusEuler.PaperLimitAgreement: For specified approximate velocities $U_j$, a finite real $T>0$ and fields $u,p$, this condition requires a smooth odd periodic Euler solution on $[0,T)$ with mean-zero pressure and smooth odd divergence-free datum $u(0)$. It requires $U_j(0)\to u(0)$ in every spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ norm and convergence in those norms uniformly on every $[0,S]$, $S<T$. The same field $u$ must be continuous on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$ and be the uniform velocity limit there. Every maximal solution of finite real lifespan from $u(0)$ must last at least to $T$ and agree with $u$ before $T$. This specifies properties; it does not prove existence. The closed-interval convergence exceeds the printed Proposition 8.1. The spatial norm is the sum of the supremum and half-Hölder seminorm of the full derivatives through order $m$.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution: On $[0,T]$, a solution here consists of a continuous curve $v$ of weakly divergence-free $C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb T^3)$ fields and a fixed divergence-free field $c$, satisfying $\mathbb P(Kv-J(\Omega v)+L)=c$ and $Jv(T)=0$. Since $Jv(0)=0$, its displacement has both zero endpoint values. The half-Hölder norm is the maximum of the supremum and seminorm. This is the projected form of (4.9); it does not yet supply a scalar pressure or prove existence. All asserted equations concern the designated interval, despite the functions being defined for every real time. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.c: Suppose a continuous divergence-free half-Hölder velocity $v$ satisfies $\mathbb P(Kv-J(\Omega v)+L)=c$ on $[0,T]$, with $T\ge0$, $K(0)=I$ and $L(0)=0$. Then $c=v(0)$, since the primitive vanishes at zero and the Leray projection fixes $v(0)$. These are the initial conditions used in §4.3 for a source obtained by integrating a force. The additional identification $c=b(0)$ uses the actual flow normalization $X_{0,0}=I$ and $D_aX_{0,0}=I$; it is not part of this algebraic conclusion. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.e: Let $T\ge0$, and let divergence-free $z,v,c$ be half-Hölder fields with continuous $v$, $z_t=v$ on $[0,T]$, and $z(0)=z(T)=0$. Suppose $Kv-J(\Omega v)+L=c+G$, where $G$ is the gradient of a differentiable periodic potential at each time. Then the same $v,c$ solve the projected endpoint equation and $z=Jv$ throughout the interval. This is a conversion of an already supplied solution, not an existence theorem for a prescribed source. Periodicity is essential for the Leray projection to remove the gradient. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.

Let $K,\Omega,L$ be time-continuous half-Hölder fields on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$. Suppose continuous divergence-free $v$ and constant $c$ satisfy $\mathbb P(Kv-J(\Omega v)+L)=c$ and $Jv(T)=0$. Then there is a periodic potential $\phi(t,\cdot)$ of zero spatial mean whose gradient $G$ is continuous in time in $C^{0,1/2}$ and satisfies $Kv-J(\Omega v)+L=c+G$. Mean zero is integration over the unit torus. This recovers the pressure gradient in (4.9). The conclusion does not assert time differentiability of the scalar potential. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.p: Suppose two integrated equations on $[0,T]$ use the same coefficients and source, their velocities agree on this interval, and their time-independent fields agree. If their remaining terms are $G_1$ and $G_2$, so that $Kv-J(\Omega v)+L=c+G_i$, then $G_1=G_2$ throughout $[0,T]$. This is the final algebraic step in pressure-gradient uniqueness for Theorems 4.2 and A.1. It assumes velocity uniqueness rather than proving it, and does not identify scalar potentials without a normalization. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent: On $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$, supply smooth matrix fields $F,M$, an inverse $G$ with $GF=FG=I$, and a continuous time derivative $M_t$. Require $F_t=MF$, $\|G\|\le D$, $\|M\|\le L$, and $\langle-(M_t+M^2)w,w\rangle\le|w|^2$ for every $w$. In §4 these are $F=D_aX$, $G=F^{-1}$ and $M=(\nabla u)\circ X$. The formal data themselves need not arise from any velocity or volume-preserving flow. They isolate the identities needed by the endpoint inverse; positivity of $T$ and bounds such as $D\ge1$ are imposed by theorems using them.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent.exists_integr: Let $T>0$ and suppose smooth periodic $F,M$ satisfy $F_t=MF$, with inverse $G$, bounds $\|G\|\le D$, $\|M\|\le L$, and $-(M_t+M^2)\le I$. For a smooth periodic label force $f_{\mathrm{lab}}(t,a)$, there is a smooth curve $L:[0,T]\to C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb T^3)$ whose values are $L(t,a)=-\int_0^tF(s,a)^Tf_{\mathrm{lab}}(s,a)\,ds$. In Theorem 4.2 one first sets $f_{\mathrm{lab}}=f\circ X$. This construction does not itself perform that composition or solve the endpoint problem.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalStepBudget.hiera: Let $\mathsf D,\lambda\ge1$ and suppose the common step coefficient has been chosen to dominate all the specified costs, including $\Gamma_P\ge1$ and an exponent $b\ge6r$. If $\Gamma_P\mathsf D^b\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$, then $(\mathsf D^r)^6\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$. This is the precise implication supplied by the formal statement behind the sentence after (5.43). The hierarchy uses loss $\mathsf D^r$ and hence its sixth power here. The assertion is a numerical consequence of the coefficient choice; it does not independently prove any hierarchy estimate or select the frequency.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution: On $[0,T]$, let $F,M$ be smooth unit-periodic matrix fields, and let $G$ satisfy $GF=FG=I$. Assume $F_t=MF$, $\|G\|\le D$, $\|M\|\le L$, and $-(M_t+M^2)\le I$. Put $K=F^TF$, $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$. For a supplied label force $f_{\rm lab}$, a smooth mean solution consists of smooth unit-periodic fields $v,z,B,\mathsf q$ satisfying $z_t=v$, $z(0)=z(T)=0$, $\operatorname{div}_av=0$, $B=Fv$ and $B_t+MB+G^T\nabla_a\mathsf q=f_{\rm lab}$ on the closed interval. These are defining conditions, not an existence assertion. No spatial mean normalization of $\mathsf q$ is imposed. An actual flow is not part of these data. Only after separately identifying $F=D_aX$, $M=DU\circ X$ and $f_{\rm lab}=f\circ X$ may one interpret $Fz$ as particle displacement and $B\circ X^{-1}$ as the Eulerian correction.

abla q=f_{\mathrm{lab}}\circ X^{-1}$. Recovering the paper's $f$ requires $f_{\mathrm{lab}}=f\circ X$.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.exist: Let $T>0$. Suppose smooth periodic matrix fields $F,M$ satisfy $F_t=MF$, have a bounded inverse, and satisfy the gradient and upper displacement-Hessian bounds used by the mean inverse. Let a smooth periodic label solution satisfy $z_t=v$, $z(0)=z(T)=0$, $\operatorname{div}_av=0$ and $B_t+MB+F^{-T}\nabla_a\mathsf q=f_{\mathrm{lab}}$, with $B=Fv$. For a smooth half-Hölder source equal to $-J(F^Tf_{\mathrm{lab}})$, this solution satisfies $\mathbb P(Kv-J(\Omega v)+L)=c$ for some time-independent solenoidal $c$, with exactly the same label velocity. The coefficient representatives must equal $F^TF$ and $F^T(M^T-M)F$. This is a compatibility result for an existing solution. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.mean_: Let $0<T\le1$ and suppose the smooth periodic parent coefficients satisfy $F_t=MF$, $G=F^{-1}$, $\|G\|\le D$ with $D\ge1$, $\|M\|\le L$ with $L\ge0$, and $-(M_t+M^2)\le I$ as quadratic forms. For the same smooth periodic forcing, take two smooth mean solutions with label displacements zero at both $0$ and $T$. The formal statement proves equality of their pulled-back physical means $B=Fz_t$ for every time in $[0,T]$. Hence their initial corrections agree. It compares existing solutions on the same interval; it does not establish existence or identify scalar pressures, whose additive time-dependent constants remain free.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.stron: Suppose smooth periodic $F,M$ obey $F_t=MF$, $G=F^{-1}$, the inverse and gradient bounds, and $-(M_t+M^2)\le I$ on $[0,T]$, $T>0$. Let a smooth periodic mean solution have $B=Fv$, zero endpoint displacement, divergence-free $v$, and $B_t+MB+G^T\nabla_a\mathsf q=f_{\mathrm{lab}}$. Then $Kv_t+\nabla_a\mathsf q=F^Tf_{\mathrm{lab}}-2F^TMFv$, with $K=F^TF$. Taking $f_{\mathrm{lab}}=f\circ X$ gives (4.11), since $2F^TMF=2F^TF_t$. The equation holds at each time, using derivatives from within the closed interval at its endpoints.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperTerminalOffOrigin: For a field $u$ and terminal time $T$, this condition requires a local $C^m$ limit for each of $u(t)$ and its time derivative, for every integer $m\ge0$ and compact $K\subset\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb Z^3$. A local limit means a $C^m$ field on an open neighbourhood of $K$ and uniform convergence on $K$ of every spatial derivative through order $m$ as $t\uparrow T$ within $[0,T)$. The lattice is the set of representatives of the torus origin. The time derivative is defined relative to the half-open lifespan. Positivity of $T$ and the Euler equations are imposed elsewhere. This condition states the two limits of Proposition 8.4 without supplying existence or a smooth continuation.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperTerminalTime: For prescribed $T,u,p$, this condition requires a smooth periodic Euler solution on $[0,T)$, with $0<T<\infty$ and mean-zero pressure, admitting no longer smooth Euler solution whose velocity agrees there. It also requires $\int_0^T\|\operatorname{curl}u(t)\|_\infty\,dt=\infty$ and $\int_0^T\|\nabla u(t)\|_\infty\,dt=\infty$. These are nonnegative Lebesgue integrals; spatial norms are essential suprema over the unit cell, and the gradient uses its operator norm. The condition does not itself identify $T$ with a limit of activation times or prove its existence. Those identifications are made when all Section 8 conclusions are established for one construction.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperTerminalVelocityCurl: For a given field $u$ and real time $T$, this condition records a single finite bound for the essential supremum of $|u(t,x)|$ over $x\in[-1/2,1/2]^3$, valid for every $0\le t<T$. It also records $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$ as $t\uparrow T$ within that interval: every prescribed threshold is exceeded at all sufficiently late times. In the periodic Euler application the cell represents $\mathbb T^3$ and $T=T_\infty>0$. The condition alone supplies neither positivity of $T$, periodicity, nor the Euler equations. Unlike the enlarged formal Proposition 8.2 conclusions, it contains no quantitative lower bound indexed by activation intervals.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperTheorem71Conclusions: For a given scheduled construction, this condition records smooth odd divergence-free periodic velocities $U_j$ on $[0,S_j]$, starting from the stationary sine shear. Residuals are bounded by $\lambda_{j+1}^{-3}$, Fourier support by $2\lambda_j^5$, and pressure Hessians above by $\sum_{i<j}\lambda_i^{-1}$ times the identity. It records the central gradient as the preceding gradient plus a switched rank-one wave and an error bounded by $\lambda_j^{-1/4}$. Crossing times have the prescribed coupling ratios and shear bounds and tend to a finite positive $T<S_j$. Oscillations are supported within distance $\lambda_{j-1}^{-1}$ of lattice points and bounded by $\lambda_j^{-1}$; the remaining increments are small in spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ for $m\le q_j$. This specifies conclusions for a construction; it does not assert existence.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff: The formal object is a real function $\widetilde\chi$ that is smooth on $[0,T]$, takes values in $[0,1]$ there, and vanishes at times $t<t_0$ within that interval. It encodes the cutoff in (3.7). The function is defined at all real times, but no restriction is imposed outside $[0,T]$, and no condition says that it eventually reaches one. For $0<t_0<T$, smoothness and vanishing to the left give flatness at activation. The first wave is treated separately by choosing $t_0=0$ and the constant function one.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.derivativeSiz: For a smooth cutoff $\widetilde\chi$ on $[0,T]$, define the real supremum $\sup_{t\in[t_0,T]}|\widetilde\chi\,{}^{\prime}(t)|\gamma(t)$. The derivative is taken within $[0,T]$, including its one-sided values at the endpoints. If $0\le t_0\le T$, $T>0$, and $\gamma$ is continuous and nonnegative, compactness makes this a finite nonnegative number, equal to the quantity $\|\widetilde\chi\,{}^{\prime}\gamma\|_\infty$ in (5.48). The definition alone does not assume those properties of $\gamma$; with signed weights it is a supremum of the displayed product, not its absolute value. The formal real supremum has a default value when the set is empty or unbounded, so boundedness is established before using it as a norm.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.first: For the first wave the formal construction chooses activation time zero and $\widetilde\chi(t)=1$ for every real $t$. This satisfies the cutoff conditions on $[0,T]$: smoothness, range in $[0,1]$ and vanishing before activation within that interval, because there are no such times in $[0,T]$. Therefore the leading wave and its curl correction are not attenuated. The cutoff derivative vanishes, so this choice contributes no activation residual in (3.8). The formula specifies the first-wave cutoff; it does not assert the same choice for later activation times.
notes.TorusEuler.ParentLabelJetBound: For a real normed-space-valued field $f$ on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$, this condition requires $\|D_a^j f(t,a)\|\le C_j\mathsf D^{pj+c}$ at every nonnegative integer order $j$ and every point. The same natural-number slope $p$ and offset $c$ apply at every order. Derivatives are multilinear maps with operator norm, including order zero. The definition asserts these inequalities but imposes no smoothness condition independently; the coefficient theorems provide smoothness and the bounds together. Proposition 5.1 uses such polynomial bounds before inserting the radius weights, and coordinate derivative sums are recovered up to order-dependent constants. At a point where a required derivative fails to exist, its formal expression is zero; the condition alone therefore does not imply smoothness.
notes.TorusEuler.ParentLabelJetBound.weighted_: All $C_j$ are nonnegative, $\mathsf D\ge1$ and $\ell_*\ge0$; the norms use multilinear derivatives, not a separately normalized coordinate sum. If $\lVert D_a^j f\rVert\le C_j\mathsf D^{pj+c}$ and $\ell_*\mathsf D^p\le1$, the weighted derivative sum is at most $(\sum_{j\le n}C_j)\mathsf D^c$. Thus the remaining exponent is independent of $n$. This is the final summation step behind (5.8); the polynomial derivative bound is an input to it.
notes.TorusEuler.RealTorusFourierBand: For a continuous real vector field on $\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$, frequency support at most $\Lambda$ means that its complex Fourier coefficient at every $\xi\in\mathbb Z^3$ with Euclidean length $|\xi|>\Lambda$ is zero. The Fourier convention is $e^{2\pi i\xi\cdot x}$. Frequencies on the boundary are permitted, and the condition does not remove the zero mode. This is the definition introduced in §5.1. The parent hypotheses use radii $2\mathsf D$ and $4\mathsf D$ for velocity and residual; the next truncated stage uses $2\Lambda$ and $4\Lambda$. The condition alone says nothing about time regularity or incompressibility.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.integrated: Let $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, $T\ge2$, $0\le t\le T$, and $\eta\ge0$. Suppose $Y$ is continuous on $[0,T]$ and $|Y|\le1$ there. With $\cos\varphi(\tau)=(1+\varepsilon^2\tau^4/4)^{-1/2}$, the formal statement proves $0\le\int_0^t(1+|Y|)^2\eta/\cos\varphi\le4T^3\eta$. The number $\eta$ here is a constant bound for an amplitude error operator, not the frozen coupling $B_{32}(t_0)$. No Riccati equation is assumed. This is the integral estimate that converts a polynomial coefficient error into a polynomial comparison error after dividing by the reference amplitude.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.log_growin: At a fixed time, let $(E_1,E_2,E_3)$ be orthonormal and $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$. Write $k=\lambda(\zeta_1E_1+\zeta_2E_2/S+\zeta_3E_3)$ and $\mathbf a=\alpha_1E_1/S+\alpha_2E_2+\alpha_3E_3/S$, with $\lambda\ne0$, $S>0$. Put $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon t^2/2)$, $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$, $h=\alpha_2/a_{\rm ref}$ and $l=-(\alpha_1+Y\alpha_2)/(a_{\rm ref}\cos\varphi)$. Assume $T\ge1$, $|\zeta_1|\le T^2$, $|\zeta_2|\le T$, $\zeta_3\ge1/2$, $|Y(t)|\le1$, and $\max\{|h-1|,|l|\}\le d\le1/2$. The formal statement gives $|\log(|\mathbf a|/a_{\rm ref})|\le2d+20T^4S^{-2}$. Closeness ensures $\alpha_2,|\mathbf a|>0$, so this logarithm has its ordinary meaning. No differential equation for $Y$ is assumed. If its formal integral is not integrable it is assigned zero; the resulting $a_{\rm ref}$ is still positive.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.orthonorma: In a real inner-product space with a three-vector orthonormal basis, suppose the coordinates of $\mathbf a$ are $(-U/S,V,(XU-QV)/(SZ))$, with $V>0$, $Z\ne0$ and $S>0$. Then $|\mathbf a|=V\sqrt{1+S^{-2}[(U/V)^2+((X(U/V)-Q)/Z)^2]}$. Taking $(X,Q,Z)=\zeta$, $U=-\alpha_1$, and $V=\alpha_2$ gives the paper’s identity $|\mathbf a|^2=\alpha_2^2+S^{-2}(\alpha_1^2+\alpha_3^2)$ after using transversality. The coordinate relations are hypotheses here. This result is purely geometric and does not require an amplitude differential equation.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.raw_ratio_: For arbitrary real functions $Y,U,V$, put $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$, $s(t)=(1+\varepsilon^2t^4/4)^{-1/2}$, $h=V/a_{\rm ref}$ and $l=(U-YV)/(s a_{\rm ref})$. If $\max\{|h(t)-1|,|l(t)|\}\le d\le1/2$, then $V(t)>0$ and $|U(t)/V(t)-Y(t)|\le2d$. Both $s$ and $a_{\rm ref}$ are positive by their definitions. For the paper’s amplitude, $U=-\alpha_1$ and $V=\alpha_2$, so the error is $|\alpha_1/\alpha_2+Y|$. No differential equation is assumed; the result extracts the ratio bound from the normalized comparison. The formal integral is assigned zero when $Y$ is not integrable, so $a_{\rm ref}=1$ at such an input; no derivative formula follows there.

Let $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$ and $s(t)=(1+\varepsilon^2t^4/4)^{-1/2}$. Define $h=V/a_{\rm ref}$ and $l=(U-YV)/(s a_{\rm ref})$. At any time with $V(t)\ne0$, the formal statement gives $U/V=Y+s\,l/h$. For $(U,V)=(-\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ this is the paper’s identity $\alpha_1/\alpha_2+Y=-l\cos\varphi/h$. The nonzero assumption makes $h\ne0$; the positive denominators $s$ and $a_{\rm ref}$ require no additional assumptions. The identity itself gives neither positivity nor a small-error estimate. The formal integral $\int_0^tY$ is assigned the value zero when $Y$ is not integrable between $0$ and $t$, so $a_{\rm ref}(t)=1$ at such a time; no derivative formula follows there.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.reference_: Let $A(t)>0$ and $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$. If $|\log(A(t)/a_{\rm ref}(t))|\le\varepsilon$, then $\exp(-\varepsilon)a_{\rm ref}(t)\le A(t)\le\exp(\varepsilon)a_{\rm ref}(t)$. The formal statement applies at one time to arbitrary functions $A,Y$; no wave equation or regularity of $Y$ is required for this implication. In Proposition 2.8, $A=|\mathbf a|$ and Lemma 2.6 supplies the positive amplitude and logarithmic bound on the whole interval. Positivity is essential for this ordinary interpretation of the logarithm. The formal integral $\int_0^tY$ is assigned the value zero when $Y$ is not integrable between $0$ and $t$, so $a_{\rm ref}(t)=1$ at such a time; no derivative formula follows there.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.hasDerivW: Put $x=\varepsilon t^2/2$, $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}=\cos\varphi$, $\varphi=\arctan x$, and $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$. Suppose $Y'=s^2(1-\varepsilon x)-2\varepsilon t x s^2Y-Y^2$ on $[0,T]$. Set $e=(Y+\varepsilon t x s^2/2)/s-1$, $h=V/a_{\rm ref}$ and $l=(U-YV)/(sa_{\rm ref})$. At $t\in[0,T]$, assume $(U,V)'=(-2\varepsilon t x s^2U+s^2(1-\varepsilon x)V,U)+R(t)(U,V)$. Let $Q(U,V)=(V,(U-YV)/s)$, so $Q^{-1}(h,l)=(Yh+sl,h)$. The formal statement gives $(h,l)'=(sl,-2s(1+e)l)+QRQ^{-1}(h,l)$ at that time. Derivatives are taken within $[0,T]$, including endpoints. This is an exact identity, with no continuity, size or sign hypothesis on the error operator $R$ at the evaluated time. The paper uses $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=(-U,V)$; the change of first sign accounts for the different off-diagonal entries.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.norm_movi: At a fixed time, let an orthonormal frame give $k=\lambda(\zeta_1E_1+\zeta_2E_2/S+\zeta_3E_3)$ and $\mathbf b=\beta_1E_1/S+\beta_2E_2+\beta_3E_3/S$. Assume $k\cdot\mathbf b=0$, $\lambda\ne0$, $S\ge1$, $|\zeta_1|,|\zeta_2|\le S$, $1/2\le\zeta_3\le3/2$, $|Y(t)|\le1$, and $|\zeta_1-\varepsilon t^2/2|\le1/2$. Put $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon t^2/2)$, $a_{\rm ref}=\exp\int_0^tY$, $h=\beta_2/a_{\rm ref}$ and $l=-(\beta_1+Y\beta_2)/(a_{\rm ref}\cos\varphi)$. The formal statement gives $|\mathbf b|\le9a_{\rm ref}\max\{|h|,|l|\}$ and $\max\{|h|,|l|\}\le7S|\mathbf b|/a_{\rm ref}$. Physical vector norms are Euclidean. No differential equation is assumed. The formal integral is zero for a nonintegrable $Y$, leaving $a_{\rm ref}>0$; for reference solutions the integral has its usual meaning.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.norm_norm: At any real time $t$, set $s=(1+\varepsilon^2t^4/4)^{-1/2}$ and $Q(U,V)=(V,(U-Y(t)V)/s)$. For any linear operator $R(t)$ on real pairs, the formal statement gives $\|QRQ^{-1}\|\le(1+|Y(t)|)^2\|R(t)\|/s$. The pair norm and its induced operator norm are maximum norms. This becomes the paper’s polynomial bound after using $|Y|\le1$, $1/s\le T^2$, and a polynomial estimate for $R$. The displayed formal result is an exact pointwise inequality for arbitrary $Y$ and $R$, so it does not itself supply those three estimates.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.normalize: For real functions $Y,U,V$, let $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$ and $s(t)=(1+\varepsilon^2t^4/4)^{-1/2}$. The formal object is $(V/a_{\rm ref},(U-YV)/(s a_{\rm ref}))$. With $U=-\alpha_1$, $V=\alpha_2$ and $s=\cos\varphi$, it is exactly $(h,l)$ from (2.15). Both denominators are strictly positive. Real pairs carry the maximum norm, so a bound on the norm of this pair is a bound on both components. The definition does not assume a reference or perturbed differential equation; such equations enter the comparison theorems. The formal integral $\int_0^tY$ is assigned the value zero when $Y$ is not integrable between $0$ and $t$, so $a_{\rm ref}(t)=1$ at such a time; no derivative formula follows there.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.unscaledC: At time $t$, put $s=(1+\varepsilon^2t^4/4)^{-1/2}$. The formal object is the linear map $Q(U,V)=(V,(U-Y(t)V)/s)$. Dividing this pair by $a_{\rm ref}(t)$ gives the normalized coordinates $(h,l)$. The paper instead writes its matrix on $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=(-U,V)$, hence its lower left entry is $-1/s$ rather than $1/s$. The maps agree after that sign change. Since $s>0$ for every real $\varepsilon,t$, the map is invertible wherever $Y(t)$ is defined. No differential equation is part of this definition. Here $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$; a nonintegrable formal integral is assigned zero. The displayed inverse relation itself uses only $Y(t)$ and $s(t)$.

At time $t$, put $s=(1+\varepsilon^2t^4/4)^{-1/2}$. The formal object maps $(h,l)$ to $(Y(t)h+sl,h)$. It is the inverse of $Q(U,V)=(V,(U-Y(t)V)/s)$; multiplying by $a_{\rm ref}$ then recovers $(U,V)$. Because $U=-\alpha_1$, the inverse matrix printed in the paper has first row $(-Y,-s)$ instead. This sign convention explains the apparent discrepancy. The positive value of $s$ makes the inverse meaningful for all real inputs, independently of whether $Y$ solves the Riccati equation. Here $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$; a nonintegrable formal integral is assigned zero. The displayed inverse relation itself uses only $Y(t)$ and $s(t)$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferencePropagator.hasDerivW: Put $x=\varepsilon t^2/2$, $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}=\cos\varphi$, $\varphi=\arctan x$, and $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$. Suppose $Y'=s^2(1-\varepsilon x)-2\varepsilon t x s^2Y-Y^2$ on $[0,T]$. Set $e=(Y+\varepsilon t x s^2/2)/s-1$, $h=V/a_{\rm ref}$ and $l=(U-YV)/(sa_{\rm ref})$. At $t\in[0,T]$, suppose $U'=-2\varepsilon t x s^2U+s^2(1-\varepsilon x)V$ and $V'=U$. The formal statement proves $h'=sl$ and $l'=-2s(1+e)l$ at that time, with derivatives taken within $[0,T]$. This is the triangular system (2.16), since $(U,V)=(-\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$. The identity requires neither $Y(0)=1$ nor positivity or smallness of $e$. The chosen arctangent makes $s>0$ for every real parameter and time, and $a_{\rm ref}>0$, so both divisions in the normalized coordinates are legitimate.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferencePropagator.normalize: Put $x=\varepsilon t^2/2$, $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}=\cos\varphi$, $\varphi=\arctan x$, and $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$. Suppose $Y'=s^2(1-\varepsilon x)-2\varepsilon t x s^2Y-Y^2$ on $[0,T]$. Assume $\varepsilon>0$, $Y(0)=1$, and $U'=-2\varepsilon t x s^2U+s^2(1-\varepsilon x)V$, $V'=U$ throughout $[0,T]$. Set $h=V/a_{\rm ref}$, $l=(U-YV)/(sa_{\rm ref})$. For every $0\le a\le b\le T$, the formal statement gives $\sqrt{h(b)^2+l(b)^2}\le2\sqrt{h(a)^2+l(a)^2}$. This is the Euclidean norm on the two normalized coordinates, not the maximum norm used in the perturbation estimates. All derivatives are relative to $[0,T]$. The constant $2$ is uniform in the times and parameter; no upper bound $\varepsilon\le1$ is assumed. In paper notation, $U=-\alpha_1$ and $V=\alpha_2$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferencePropagator.triangula: Let $a\le b$, and let $s,e$ be continuous and nonnegative on $[a,b]$. Set $d(a,t)=\exp(-\int_a^t2s(1+e))$ and $q(a,b)=\int_a^b s(t)d(a,t)\,dt$. The formal statement gives $0<d(a,b)\le1$ and $0\le q(a,b)\le(1-d(a,b))/2$. Thus the transfer from $l$ into $h$ is bounded by half the decrease of its absolute amplitude. The result applies to arbitrary continuous nonnegative coefficients, including $s=\cos\varphi$ and the reference deviation. It estimates coefficients of the explicit solution formula and does not itself quantify over solutions.

Let $a\le b$, with continuous nonnegative functions $s,e$ on $[a,b]$. Suppose $h\prime=sl$ and $l'=-2s(1+e)l$ throughout that interval, using one-sided derivatives at the endpoints. Then $|h(b)|+|l(b)|\le|h(a)|+|l(a)|$. This is the contraction used in Section 2.2.2 with $s=\cos\varphi$ and the bounded deviation of the reference solution. The formal statement is more general than that specialization: neither a Riccati equation nor bounds on $\varepsilon$ appear, because nonnegativity of the two coefficient functions is the only property needed here.

Let $s,e$ be continuous on $[a,b]$, and let $h,l$ satisfy $h\prime=sl$, $l'=-2s(1+e)l$ there. For $t\in[a,b]$, set $d(a,t)=\exp(-\int_a^t2s(1+e))$ and $q(a,t)=\int_a^t s(u)d(a,u)\,du$. The formal statement gives $l(t)=d(a,t)l(a)$ and $h(t)=h(a)+q(a,t)l(a)$. The result uses derivatives within the closed interval and permits coefficients of either sign. Decay and contraction require the separate nonnegativity hypotheses used later. With $s=\cos\varphi$, this is the solution formula behind (2.16).
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.actual_coupl:
Let $0<\varepsilon\le1/16$, $T\ge2$, $x=\varepsilon	au^2/2$, $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}=\cos\varphi$ and $\varphi=\arctan x$. Suppose $Y=s(1+e)-\varepsilon	au x s^2/2$, with $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$ on $[0,\infty)$. Define $n_0=(x+\varepsilon+2\varepsilon	au Y)s$ and $h_0=(-1+\varepsilon x+2(1+x^2)Y^2+2\varepsilon	au xY)s$. If scalar functions $n,h$ satisfy $|n-n_0|,|h-h_0|\le\varepsilon/(8T^2)$ on $[0,T]$, then $n\ge\varepsilon/2$ there. For $\sqrt2/\varepsilon\le	au\le T$, the formal statement gives $|n-1|\le\varepsilon$ and $|(h/n)/s-1|\le1/2$. In the application, $n=
u_+/
u$ and $h=\eta_+/
u$. This result assumes the additive comparison; it neither constructs a wave nor requires a differential equation for $Y$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.amplitude_in: Let $Y$ be continuous on $[0,\infty)$, with $Y\le1$, and suppose $\int_0^{\tau_m}Y\ge\varepsilon^{-1/2}-1$. Assume $2\varepsilon\le1$, $\tau_m\in[0,T]$, and $\exp(-\varepsilon)a_{\rm ref}\le A\le\exp(\varepsilon)a_{\rm ref}$ on $[0,T]$, where $a_{\rm ref}=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$. For $\tau\in[0,1]$ with $\tau\le T$, the formal statement proves $A(\tau)\le\exp(3-\varepsilon^{-1/2})A(\tau_m)$. This is slightly sharper than replacing $A(\tau_m)$ by the maximum over $[0,T]$. The formal expression $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$ means $1/\sqrt\varepsilon$; the application has $\varepsilon>0$. There is no positivity hypothesis on $\varepsilon$ in this statement. Its formal real square root, and hence its reciprocal, is zero for $\varepsilon\le0$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.amplitude_la: Let $0<\varepsilon\le1$, $\tau_m\in[2/\varepsilon,3/\varepsilon]$ and $\tau_m\le\tau\le T$. Put $x(t)=\varepsilon t^2/2$, $s(t)=(1+x(t)^2)^{-1/2}$. Suppose $Y$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ and $Y=s(1+e)-\varepsilon t x s^2/2$, with $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$ there. Define $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$. Assume $a_{\rm ref}(t)\le a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)$ and $ca_{\rm ref}(t)\le A(t)\le Ca_{\rm ref}(t)$ for $0\le t\le T$, where $c,C>0$, and assume an attained maximum $M=\max_{[0,T]}A$. If $k_{\min},k_{\max}\ge0$ and $k_{\min}x(\tau)\le k\le k_{\max}x(\tau)$, then $k_{\min}(c/C)\sqrt{x(\tau)/\varepsilon}\le kA(\tau)/M\le3\exp(2)k_{\max}(C/c)\sqrt{x(\tau)/\varepsilon}$. Here $k$ is a scalar, representing $|k(\tau)|/\lambda$ in the application. The maximum and amplitude comparisons are hypotheses.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.amplitude_ra: Let $c,C>0$, $\tau_m,\tau\in[0,T]$, and $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$. Suppose $a_{\rm ref}(t)\le a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)$ on $[0,T]$ and $ca_{\rm ref}(t)\le A(t)\le Ca_{\rm ref}(t)$ there. If $M$ is an attained maximum of $A$ on that interval, then $(c/C)a_{\rm ref}(\tau)/a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)\le A(\tau)/M\le(C/c)a_{\rm ref}(\tau)/a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)$. The positivity assumptions ensure nonzero denominators. The formal statement assumes existence of $M$ and the reference maximum; it does not prove either. In the crossing argument, $A=|\mathbf a|$ and $c,C=\exp(\mp\varepsilon)$. The formal integral $\int_0^tY$ is assigned the value zero when $Y$ is not integrable between $0$ and $t$, so $a_{\rm ref}(t)=1$ at such a time; no derivative formula follows there.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.couplingRati: Let $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2\ge1$, $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}$, and suppose a real number $\rho$ satisfies $|\rho/s-1|\le1/2$. Then $1/(4x)\le\rho\le3/(2x)$. In Proposition 2.8, $s=\cos\varphi$ and $\rho=\eta_+/\nu_+$. The hypothesis $x\ge1$ makes all reciprocals positive. The formal statement is an algebraic consequence of the relative comparison; it does not require continuity or prove a crossing, which use this estimate on an interval.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.coupling_err: Assume $T\ge2$, $\delta\ge0$, and nonnegative integers $p,C_0$ with $p+2\le C_0$. Let a real coefficient $C$ satisfy $8C\le C_0$. If $C_0T^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$, then $CT^p\delta\le\varepsilon/(8T^2)$. This is the precise arithmetic step used to obtain the coupling error margin in Section 2.2.4 from (2.7). The exponents are natural numbers; the formal statement does not quantify over arbitrary real exponents. It imposes no positivity on $C$, although the application uses a nonnegative error constant.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.deviation_ex: For $0<\varepsilon\le1$ and $\varphi(\tau)=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$, the formal statement constructs a real function $e$ with $e(0)=0$, $e'=\cos\varphi[-2e-e^2+(\varepsilon/2)\sin\varphi\cos\varphi]$ on $[0,\infty)$, and $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$ there. Derivatives at zero are taken from the right. The function is defined at negative times too, but the equation and bound impose no conditions there. This is existence with an invariant interval for the deviation; uniqueness and the corresponding Riccati solution $Y$ are not conclusions of this declaration.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.deviation_ze: For real $\varepsilon$ and a function $Y$ with $Y(0)=1$, define $e(\tau)=[Y(\tau)+\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4]/\cos\varphi-1$, with $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$. The formal statement proves $e(0)=0$, since $\varphi(0)=0$. It uses only the initial value of $Y$, not its differential equation or continuity. This supplies the initial condition in the deviation equation derived in the proof of Lemma 2.5; the evolution and interval bound for $e$ are separate conclusions.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.hasDerivAt_s: For arbitrary real $\varepsilon,\tau$, let $s(\tau)=(1+\varepsilon^2\tau^4/4)^{-1/2}=\cos\varphi(\tau)$, where $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$. The formal statement gives $s'=-(\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/2)s$. Since $s>0$, division by $s$ yields $(\log\cos\varphi)\prime=-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/2$. The displayed formal conclusion is the derivative of $s$ itself; it does not separately state the derivative of $\varphi$ or of its logarithm. No Riccati solution or positive-parameter hypothesis is needed.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.hasDerivWith: Let $\varphi(\tau)=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$ and suppose $Y'=\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)Y-Y^2$ at a given time. Define $e=[Y+\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4]/\cos\varphi-1$. The formal statement gives $e'=\cos\varphi[-2e-e^2+(\varepsilon/2)\sin\varphi\cos\varphi]$ at that time. The derivative may be restricted to an arbitrary time set, so the same calculation covers one-sided endpoint derivatives. The initial condition $e(0)=0$ requires $Y(0)=1$ separately, and no invariant-interval bound is asserted here.

Let $Y$ be continuous on $[0,\infty)$ and set $a_{\rm ref}(\tau)=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$. For every $\tau\ge0$, the formal statement proves $a_{\rm ref}\prime(\tau)=Y(\tau)a_{\rm ref}(\tau)$, with a right derivative at zero. Its named first reference component is $U=Ya_{\rm ref}$; the paper’s first amplitude component is $\alpha_1=-U$, so this derivative also says $\alpha_2\prime=-\alpha_1$. The result requires continuity but not the Riccati equation. Positivity of the exponential makes $Y=a_{\rm ref}\prime/a_{\rm ref}$ legitimate.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.inv_sq_windo: Assume $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, $T\ge2$ and $0\le\tau\le T$. Then $(1+\varepsilon^2\tau^4/4)^{-1/2}\ge T^{-2}$. Since this quantity equals $\cos\varphi$ for $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$, the inequality is equivalent to $1/\cos\varphi\le T^2$. This is the polynomial denominator bound used when conjugating the amplitude error in Section 2.2.3. The formal statement uses only the parameter and time bounds; it is independent of the wave, the Riccati solution and the coefficient error.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.inv_two_mul_: Put $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$ and assume $x\ge1$. The formal statement proves $(2x)^{-1}\le(1+x^2)^{-1/2}$. With $x=\tan\varphi$ and $\varphi=\arctan x$, this is $1/(2\tan\varphi)\le\cos\varphi$, the lower comparison used after the reference peak. Only $x\ge1$ is required; no independent positivity assumption on $\varepsilon$ or time bound is stated. The hypothesis makes all denominators nonzero and positive.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceEta: For real $\varepsilon,\tau$ and a function $Y$, put $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$ and $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}$. The formal object is $h_0=[-1+\varepsilon x+2(1+x^2)Y(\tau)^2+2\varepsilon\tau xY(\tau)]s$. With $x=\tan\varphi$, this is the unreduced reference value of $\eta_+/\nu$ in Section 2.2.4. It is not the ratio $\eta_+/\nu_+$; that requires division by the first reference coupling. The definition assumes no Riccati equation or smallness, so the cancellation and late-time estimates require the representation and bound for $Y$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceNu:
For real $\varepsilon,	au$ and a function $Y$, set $x=\varepsilon	au^2/2$, $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}$. The formal object is $n_0=(x+\varepsilon+2\varepsilon	au Y(	au))s$. In the reference wave this equals $\sin\varphi+\varepsilon\cos\varphi+2\varepsilon	au Y\cos\varphi$, the normalized value $
u_+/
u$ used in Section 2.2.4. Thus it is dimensionless, not the physical coupling $
u_+$ itself. At $	au=0$ it equals $\varepsilon$ for every $Y$. Positivity at later times and the late bound near one are additional results.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceNu_: Let $0<\varepsilon\le1$, $0\le\tau\le\sqrt2/\varepsilon$, and $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$. Suppose $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4$ and $e(\tau)\ge0$. Then the reference expression $\sin\varphi+\varepsilon\cos\varphi+2\varepsilon\tau Y\cos\varphi$ is at least $\varepsilon$. This is the lower bound for $\nu_+/\nu$ in the early range of Lemma 2.7. The formal statement does not need the upper bound $e\le\varepsilon/8$ or a differential equation for $Y$; it uses only the representation and nonnegativity at this time.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceU_z: Assume $Y(0)=1$ and define $a_{\rm ref}(\tau)=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$, $U=Ya_{\rm ref}$. The formal statement gives $U(0)=1$, because the integral over $[0,0]$ is zero. In the paper, $U=-\alpha_1$, so the corresponding initial value is $\alpha_1(0)=-1$. This one-coordinate equality is only part of the reference initial data $(-1,1)$; the second component is established separately. No regularity or Riccati equation for $Y$ is needed for this initial-value calculation.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceV: For a real function $Y$, the formal object is $a_{\rm ref}(\tau)=\exp(\int_0^\tau Y(t)\,dt)$. It is positive and equals one at zero. When $Y$ is continuous on the nonnegative half-line, its derivative is $Ya_{\rm ref}$ there, and a Riccati solution gives the reference amplitude of Lemma 2.5. The definition accepts all real times and all functions. The interval integral is oriented for negative upper limits and assigned zero for nonintegrable integrands; regularity assumptions in the reference theorem ensure the ordinary integral interpretation on $\tau\ge0$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceV_l: Let $a\ge0$ and let $Y$ be continuous on $[0,\infty)$, with $Y\ge0$ on $[0,a]$ and $Y\le0$ on $[a,\infty)$. Then $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$ satisfies $a_{\rm ref}(t)\le a_{\rm ref}(a)$ for every $t\ge0$. The paper applies this with $a=\tau_m$, the unique zero of its reference slope. The formal statement requires only weak sign inequalities and does not assert uniqueness of the maximum or require a Riccati equation. The strict signs supplied by Lemma 2.5 are more than this step needs.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceV_r: Let $\varphi(t)=\arctan(\varepsilon t^2/2)$ and suppose $Y$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ with $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon t\sin(2\varphi)/4$. For $0\le a\le b$, put $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$. The formal statement proves $a_{\rm ref}(b)/a_{\rm ref}(a)=\sqrt{\cos\varphi(b)/\cos\varphi(a)}\exp\int_a^b(1+e)\cos\varphi$. This is the ratio formula used after the reference peak, but the theorem applies to any ordered nonnegative times. Neither the Riccati equation, positivity of $\varepsilon$, nor bounds on $e$ are required for this identity.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceV_z: For any real function $Y$, set $a_{\rm ref}(\tau)=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$. The formal statement gives $a_{\rm ref}(0)=1$. It needs no continuity, integrability or differential equation because the interval has zero length. This is the second component $\alpha_2(0)=1$ of the reference initial data in Section 2.2.2. It does not state the first initial component or assert that this function solves the amplitude equation; those require further identities and the relevant regularity assumptions.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceY: For arbitrary real $\varepsilon$ and a real function $e$, the formal object is $Y(\tau)=(1+e(\tau))s(\tau)-\varepsilon\tau x(\tau)s(\tau)^2/2$, where $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$ and $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}$. With $s=\cos\varphi$ and $xs=\sin\varphi$, this is (2.13): $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4$. The definition places no bound or differential equation on $e$. Thus the formula alone supplies neither $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$ nor a solution of (2.12); those are separate assertions in Lemma 2.5.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceY_n: Let $0<\varepsilon\le1$ and $\varepsilon\tau=3$. Suppose $e(\tau)\le\varepsilon/8$ and set $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$, $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4$. The formal statement proves $Y(\tau)<0$. No differential equation or lower bound on $e$ is needed for this pointwise sign calculation. This gives the upper sign in the proof that the reference amplitude peaks between $2/\varepsilon$ and $3/\varepsilon$; existence and uniqueness of that peak require the later Riccati argument.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceY_p: Assume $\varepsilon\ge0$, $\varepsilon\tau\le2$, and $e(\tau)\ge0$. For $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$, the formal statement proves $(1+e(\tau))\cos\varphi-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4>0$. Applied to the deviation of the reference Riccati solution for $\tau\ge0$, this is the positive sign before the reference peak in Lemma 2.5. The algebraic statement itself also permits negative $\tau$ and $\varepsilon=0$ and needs no differential equation or upper bound on $e$. Its extra domain does not extend the Riccati existence theorem to negative time.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.reference_am: Let $\varepsilon\in\mathbb R$, $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$, $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}=\cos\varphi$ and $\varphi=\arctan x$. Suppose $Y'=s^2(1-\varepsilon x)-2\varepsilon\tau x s^2Y-Y^2$ on $[0,\infty)$. Define $V(\tau)=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$ and $U(\tau)=Y(\tau)V(\tau)$. The formal statement proves $V'=U$ and $U'=s^2(1-\varepsilon x)V-2\varepsilon\tau x s^2U$ for every $\tau\ge0$, with right derivatives at zero. These are (2.5) in the coordinates $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=(-U,V)$. No condition $Y(0)=1$ is assumed. The reconstruction always has $V(0)=1$, while the paper’s initial pair $(-1,1)$ additionally requires $Y(0)=1$. Values at negative times are not constrained by the differential-equation hypothesis.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.reference_co:
Let $0<\varepsilon\le1$, $	au\ge\sqrt2/\varepsilon$, $x=\varepsilon	au^2/2$ and $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}=\cos\varphi$, where $\varphi=\arctan x$. Suppose $Y=s(1+e)-\varepsilon	au x s^2/2$ and $0\le e(	au)\le\varepsilon/8$. Define $n_0=(x+\varepsilon+2\varepsilon	au Y)s$ and $h_0=(-1+\varepsilon x+2(1+x^2)Y^2+2\varepsilon	au xY)s$. The formal statement proves $|n_0-1|\le7\varepsilon^2$ and $|h_0/s-1|\le2\varepsilon$. These are explicit reference estimates following (2.22). The functions represent $
u_+/
